bib.title: 10 Graph feature engineering: Manual and semiautomated approaches (Knowledge Graphs and LLMs in Action)
authors: Negro et al. (not printed in the chapter text; taken from the repo notes)

question: How do we turn nodes and relationships of a graph into interpretable feature vectors for classical ML, by hand and with the semiautomated ReFeX algorithm?
contributions: Manual node features (degree, triangles, egonet density, geodesic paths, closeness, betweenness, PageRank) with fraud-aware variants and NetworkX code on a 20-node toy fraud graph
Relationship features: node-vector combinations (catenate, average, L1, L2, Hadamard) and path-based metapath/DWPC features for drug repurposing on Hetionet
ReFeX walkthrough by hand and in code as a semiautomated, interpretable feature extractor

limits: No benchmark or metric is reported anywhere; the fraud example is a 20-node toy and the authors say its results are not statistically relevant.
The ReFeX section cannot use node attributes or edge types, and pruning sometimes needs human oversight (stated by the authors).
Manual features are labor-intensive, need domain expertise and customisation per use case.
Calculating geodesic paths is computationally expensive; manual computation is infeasible on real networks.
DWPC over all pairs and metapaths is expensive and noisy; the chapter relies on Himmelstein et al. for the reduction and gives no numbers for classifier quality.
No choice rule is given for the node-vector combination operator: 'There is no generic rule'; benchmark it.
The LLM-assisted Cypher generation is an untested prompt illustration.
practices: Build node features incrementally from local (degree, triangles, egonet density) to global (geodesic, closeness, betweenness, PageRank) and iterate until the classifier is good enough (Sections 10.1, 10.1.8).
Split degree, triangle and path features into fraud and legit variants so they carry domain meaning (10.1.1, 10.1.2, 10.1.4).
Compare base PageRank with fraud-weighted PageRank and investigate nodes whose weighted rank rises much above the base rank (10.1.7).
Use a stratified train/test split and scale features before logistic regression (Listing 10.11).
Choose the node-vector combination operator by benchmarking on your scenario (10.2.1).
Use degree-weighted path counts rather than raw path counts so hub nodes do not dominate (10.2.2).
Reduce metapaths and candidate pairs using statistical and domain knowledge before computing DWPC for all pairs (10.2.2).
Use an LLM to draft Cypher for metapath queries from the schema, one example query, the metapath list and sample names (10.2.2 box).
Use ReFeX when interpretability and cross-graph or over-time comparability matter and the graph is too large for hand features (10.3).
Keep a domain expert in the loop to validate generated ReFeX features (10.3).

terms.definition: a particular node and its immediate neighbors; the center is the ego and the surrounding nodes are the alters
features extracted from the node's one-hop (or n-order) neighborhood
measures of the role of each node in the entire network, such as betweenness, closeness, PageRank, eigenvector centrality
number of fraudulent / legitimate direct neighbors
a triangle in which only one of the two alters is fraudulent
the inverse of farness, where farness is the mean geodesic distance from a node to all others; unreachable nodes are excluded
how often a node appears on shortest paths between other pairs of nodes
given two nodes, how likely a relationship exists between them; binary (exists) or multiclass (which type)
a typed path pattern through the schema, such as Compound-binds-Gene-associates-Disease (CbGaD)
degree-weighted path count: path counts with each path damped by the degrees of its intermediate nodes
Recursive Feature eXtraction: recursively combines local and egonet features with neighborhood aggregates (sum, mean), then prunes
